query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) into high-entropy alloys will enable in situ formation of a lubricious Mo-oxide (e.g., MoO2) tribolayer during sliding, thereby simultaneously reducing the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy (e.g., a CoCrFeMnNi‐based alloy) without Mo addition that exhibits standard friction coefficients and wear rates under typical operating conditions.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by doping with a moderate concentration of Mo (using a similar approach as in Mo-incorporated (AlCrTiZrMox)N coatings).
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted under controlled normal loads and sliding speeds over a broad temperature range (e.g., from room temperature to several hundred degrees Celsius) in an ambient or low-oxygen environment that allows controlled oxide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a shearable, layered Mo-oxide tribolayer (such as MoO2) at the friction interface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, frictional heat promotes the oxidation of Mo, leading to the self-formation of a lamellar Mo-oxide film at the contact interface. This layer acts as a solid lubricant by reducing shear strength between surfaces, while the combination of enhanced hardness and toughness from the Mo addition also reduces material removal, thereby lowering both the coefficient of friction and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Mo-doped alloy is predicted to show a markedly lower friction coefficient (potentially decreasing by more than 50%) and a significantly reduced wear rate (up to an order of magnitude decrease), with these improvements sustained over the broad temperature range examined.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy typically exhibits higher friction coefficients (e.g., around 0.70 or above) and wear rates that are standard for sliding contacts without added solid lubricants.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected as long as the Mo content remains within an optimal range that promotes controlled oxide formation without compromising the alloy’s structural integrity. Extreme environments that prevent Mo oxidation or excessively high Mo levels that might form brittle phases could limit the effectiveness of this intervention.
generation.uncertainty: Precise Mo concentration for optimal tribolayer formation and the exact trade-off between enhanced oxidation for lubrication versus any potential adverse effects on alloy toughness remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the standard composition and a test set with a moderate Mo addition. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding tests across a wide range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature up to 600°C) under controlled normal load and speed conditions. Characterize the friction coefficient and wear rate continuously and perform post-test surface analyses (SEM, EDS, and XRD) to detect the presence and quality of the Mo-oxide tribolayer.
measurements: Quantification of wear volume via surface profilometry
Microstructural and compositional analysis of worn surfaces to confirm the presence of Mo-oxide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate (e.g., less than 50% reduction in friction and no order-of-magnitude improvement in wear rate) relative to the untreated alloy across the temperature range, or if no Mo-rich lubricious oxide layer is detected on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Traditional friction theory holds that the strength and fracture toughness of materials determine the wear rate [,]. During the friction process, materials with high strength minimize wear by reducing the contact area, while high-toughness materials reduce the risk of brittle fracture owing to uniform plastic deformation [,]. Although hardness and toughness always rise and fall in a lever-like manner, they are equally important for the wear resistance of materials [,]. Banerjee et al. found that the coating with medium hardness showed the best wear resistance, while the coating with the highest hardness showed brittle characteristics []. Wang et al. found that the CrBCN-L coating with the lowest hardness (17.9 GPa) but the best toughness (KIC = 2.81 MPa m1/2) showed the best wear resistance (wear rate = 2.4 × 10−7 mm3/(N·m)) []. Therefore, overcoming the tradeoff between the fracture toughness and hardness of materials has become an effective way of enhancing the wear resistance of materials. Furthermore, previous studies have shown that the oxide of Mo has a layered structure and is easy to shear, which helps to promote the wear resistance of the material [,].
